24851:
Abraham, first called Abram, is the founding father of Israel and a spiritual ancestor claimed by Jews, Christians and Muslims. Genesis 12 opens his story with God's call to leave his country and family for a land God would show him, attached to sweeping promises: a great nation, a great name, the land of Canaan for his offspring, and blessing through him for all the families of the earth. At seventy-five he goes, with his barren wife Sarai and his nephew Lot.

The narrative that follows tests whether Abraham will trust those promises when everything seems against them. He believes God and it is counted to him as righteousness (Gen 15:6), receives covenants sealed by a solemn ceremony and by circumcision, and intercedes boldly for Sodom. Yet he also twice passes off his wife as his sister to protect himself, and he takes Hagar as a surrogate when the promised child is slow in coming. The son of promise, Isaac, is born when Abraham is a hundred, and the climax comes when God commands him to offer Isaac on Moriah and then provides a ram in his place.

Abraham dies owning only a burial cave in the land promised to him, yet later Scripture treats him as the model of faith. The prophets appeal to him as God's friend; Paul argues that his faith before circumcision makes him the father of all who believe, Jew and Gentile (Rom 4); James highlights the obedience that completed his faith (Jas 2:21-23); and Hebrews remembers him as a stranger looking for a city whose builder is God (Heb 11:8-19).
24852: Genesis records Abram's origin in Ur and Haran (Gen 11:27-32), God's call and promises (Gen 12:1-3), his journeys through Canaan and Egypt (Gen 12-13), his rescue of Lot and meeting with Melchizedek (Gen 14), God's covenant oath and Abram's credited faith (Gen 15), Ishmael's birth (Gen 16), the renaming and circumcision covenant (Gen 17), the visitors at Mamre and intercession for Sodom (Gen 18), the Gerar episode (Gen 20), Isaac's birth and Ishmael's departure (Gen 21), the binding of Isaac (Gen 22), Sarah's burial (Gen 23), the search for Rebekah (Gen 24), and his death at 175 (Gen 25:7-10). The New Testament cites him as justified by faith (Rom 4:1-25, Gal 3:6-9), as acting on faith (Heb 11:8-19), as justified by works that completed his faith (Jas 2:21-23), and as rejoicing to see Christ's day (John 8:56). Jesus speaks of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob at the feast of the kingdom (Matt 8:11).

The Mishnah lists ten trials he withstood (m. Avot 5:3). The Akedah (binding of Isaac) is central to Rosh Hashanah liturgy as an appeal to Abraham's merit and God's mercy.

24918:
Sarah, first called Sarai, is the wife of Abraham and the first matriarch of Israel. Genesis introduces her with a single stark fact: she was barren and had no child (Gen 11:30). The whole promise to Abraham of a great nation therefore hangs on her, and the narrative repeatedly puts that promise at risk, once in Pharaoh's palace and again in Abimelech's court, when Abraham presents her as his sister.

Sarah's own initiatives are mixed. She gives her servant Hagar to Abraham to obtain a child through her, then turns on Hagar when the plan breeds contempt. When God renames her and the visitors at Mamre announce she will bear a son within a year, she laughs in disbelief. Yet she does bear Isaac at ninety, names her joy in him as laughter from God, and later insists that Isaac alone be the heir, a demand God tells Abraham to heed.

Sarah dies at Hebron, and Abraham's purchase of her burial cave becomes Israel's first foothold in the promised land. The New Testament remembers her as one who received strength to conceive because she judged God faithful (Heb 11:11), as a model of holy women who hoped in God (1 Pet 3:5-6), and as the free woman in Paul's allegory of two covenants (Gal 4:21-31).
24919: Sarai is Abram's wife and barren (Gen 11:29-30). Abraham later says she is his half-sister, daughter of his father but not his mother (Gen 20:12). She is taken by Pharaoh (Gen 12:15) and by Abimelech (Gen 20:2) and returned. She gives Hagar to Abram (Gen 16:2-3), is renamed and promised a son (Gen 17:15-16), laughs (Gen 18:12), bears Isaac (Gen 21:1-7), demands Ishmael's expulsion (Gen 21:10), and dies at 127 (Gen 23:1). Isaiah calls Israel to look to Sarah who bore them (Isa 51:2). Paul uses her as the free woman (Gal 4:22-31) and cites the promise of a son to her (Rom 9:9). Hebrews and 1 Peter praise her faith and hope (Heb 11:11, 1 Pet 3:6).
